strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: outlier suppression for low-bit activation quantization of diffusion models, where existing PTQ/QAT methods struggle at W4A4/W4A3.

The core technical idea—Single Hadamard Transformation applied only to activations (as opposed to the conventional Double Hadamard Transformation that also transforms weights offline)—is a reasonable and well-motivated design choice, explicitly analyzed via the outlier-diffusion property of Hadamard matrices (Eq. 19-20) and supported by empirical weight-outlier visualizations (Fig. 3c).

The proposed scheme explicitly targets two concrete limitations of prior Hadamard-based quantization (QuaRot, Xi et al.): incompatibility with integer convolution and amplification of weight outliers, offering a plausible and hardware-motivated justification for the design.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation across three datasets (ImageNet 256x256, LSUN-Bedrooms, LSUN-Churches) and multiple bit-width configurations (W8A8 down to W4A3), with consistent metrics (IS, FID, sFID, Precision, Recall).
Ablation study on Hadamard matrix order k provides some insight into a key hyperparameter.
Training convergence curves (Fig. 4) and qualitative visual comparisons (Figs. 11-14) support the claim of more stable/faster QAT convergence and improved visual fidelity at aggressive bit-widths.

Channel-wise activation visualizations (Figs. 2, 5-10) provide reasonably convincing qualitative evidence that the Hadamard transform reduces per-channel activation outliers across blocks and timesteps.
weaknesses: The headline improvement figures are misleading: the reported 467.73% IS improvement at W4A3 stems from an apparently catastrophically broken EfficientDM baseline (IS=8.74, FID=99.78), which looks like a training/configuration failure rather than a genuine, fair comparison point; relying on such a degenerate baseline to report large percentage gains overstates the practical significance of the method.

At the more standard W4A4 setting, gains are modest and mixed: IS improves by ~12.8% but FID is roughly on par with EfficientDM (6.58 vs 6.63), and on ImageNet W4A8/W8A4 HQ-DM is sometimes slightly worse than EfficientDM (e.g., 8/8 IS 363.22 vs 363.71, 4/8 IS 350.22 vs 351.97), which tempers the strength of the overall claims.

No direct empirical comparison against QuaRot or Xi et al.'s Double Hadamard Transformation baseline under the same QAT/diffusion setting, despite these being the closest related works and the primary point of differentiation; the comparison remains largely conceptual/qualitative (Fig. 3) rather than a controlled ablation isolating Single vs Double Hadamard under identical training conditions.

"Hardware-friendly" and integer-arithmetic efficiency claims are argued theoretically but never validated with actual latency, throughput, or memory measurements on real hardware, leaving the practical benefit unverified.

The method is largely built on the existing EfficientDM LoRA-distillation and LSQ timestep-aware quantization pipeline; the core novel component is restricted to the choice of applying Hadamard transform to activations only, which, while sensible, is an incremental modification rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution.

Missing comparisons with several other recent diffusion-quantization baselines discussed in the related work (e.g., DMQ, MPQ-DM, QuEST across all settings) that could contextualize how large or state-of-the-art the reported gains truly are.

No reported variance/multiple-run statistics for the stochastic generative metrics (IS/FID), making it hard to assess whether reported gains at borderline settings (e.g., W4A4) are statistically meaningful versus within normal run-to-run variation.

The trade-off from switching to symmetric quantization (sacrificing ~1 bit of effective range for hardware compatibility) is asserted but not quantitatively isolated via ablation against asymmetric quantization under the same Hadamard scheme.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation and some redundant/duplicate citations (e.g., ref [23] and [24] refer to the same TFMQ-DM paper), and could benefit from clearer organization of the single vs double Hadamard trade-off argument.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: activation outliers under aggressive low-bit QAT for diffusion models, situated clearly within relevant prior work (QuaRot, Xi et al., EfficientDM).

The core technical idea—applying the Hadamard transform only to activations (Single Hadamard) rather than to both sides (Double Hadamard)—is a sensible and reasonably well-motivated design choice, with a clear analytical argument (Eq. 19-20) for why transforming weights can amplify outliers and why it precludes efficient integer convolution.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across three datasets (ImageNet, LSUN-Bedrooms, LSUN-Churches) and multiple bit-width configurations (W8A8 down to W4A3), with consistent qualitative trend that gains grow as activation bit-width shrinks.
Channel-wise outlier visualizations (Fig. 2, 5-10) provide reasonably convincing qualitative evidence that the Hadamard transform flattens activation outliers across blocks and timesteps.
Ablation on Hadamard block order k is a useful sanity check showing the method is not overly sensitive to this hyperparameter.
Method retains symmetric quantization for hardware-friendliness, an explicit and reasonable design trade-off that is discussed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The headline '467.73% IS improvement' claim at W4A3 is misleading: the EfficientDM baseline at this setting is essentially broken (IS=8.74, FID=99.78), so any functioning model yields an enormous relative improvement while the absolute HQ-DM result (IS=49.62 vs. FP=365.35, FID=33.47) remains far from usable quality. Framing this as a headline result overstates practical significance.

One of the three claimed contributions—the superiority of Single over Double Hadamard Transformation—is only supported qualitatively (Fig. 3c, illustrating weight-outlier amplification) rather than via a controlled empirical ablation that implements Double Hadamard within the same QAT/distillation pipeline and directly compares end-task metrics. Without this apples-to-apples comparison, the central architectural claim rests on visual intuition rather than direct evidence.

No latency, throughput, or actual integer-hardware deployment measurements are reported despite repeated claims of being a 'hardware-efficient'/'hardware-friendly' scheme; the efficiency argument is entirely theoretical (integer arithmetic compatibility) and unverified in practice.

Comparisons omit several recent competitive PTQ methods discussed in Related Work (DMQ, MPQ-DM, So et al.) even though they are directly relevant to low-bit diffusion quantization; several table rows for existing baselines (Q-Diffusion, PTQD, TFMQ-DM) are marked '–' rather than measured, weakening the comprehensiveness of the comparison.

Results are mixed at higher bit-widths (e.g., W8A4: HQ-DM has worse FID than EfficientDM, 7.68 vs 6.75), and the paper does not analyze or discuss these cases where the method underperforms, focusing narrative only on favorable low-bit regimes.

No ablation isolating the effect of symmetric vs. asymmetric activation quantization within the proposed framework, despite explicitly acknowledging this trade-off costs roughly one bit of effective quantization range.

Evaluation is confined to older LDM/DDIM architectures; no experiments on more modern diffusion backbones (e.g., DiT-style or text-to-image latent diffusion models) limit confidence in generalizability of the approach.
Minor presentation issues: duplicate references (e.g., LSQ cited as both [12] and [13]; TFMQ-DM as [23] and [24]) suggest insufficient proofreading.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practical problem: activation outliers in low-bit QAT for diffusion models, building on established Hadamard transformation ideas but tailoring them to the convolutional and iterative nature of diffusion model inference.

The proposed Single Hadamard Transformation is a clear, well-motivated modification over the conventional Double Hadamard Transformation, with a good theoretical explanation (Eq. 15-16 and surrounding analysis) of why offline weight-side transformation amplifies weight outliers and breaks integer convolution support.

Extensive experiments across multiple datasets (ImageNet, LSUN-Bedrooms, LSUN-Churches) and architectures (LDM U-Net and DiT Transformer), and across a range of bit-widths (8/8 down to 4/3), showing consistent improvements over EfficientDM and other PTQ baselines, especially pronounced at very low activation bit-widths (W4A3).

Ablation studies (Table 5, Table 6) reasonably isolate the contribution of LSQ, LoRA, and the Hadamard transformation component, and directly compare Single vs Double Hadamard Transformation, supporting the core technical claims.

Reports training efficiency and inference latency numbers, providing some practical evidence that the approach doesn't introduce prohibitive overhead relative to EfficientDM and enjoys speedup relative to Double Hadamard variant.
Analysis figures (Fig. 2 and Fig. 4) provide reasonably direct empirical visualization of outlier reduction/introduction effects that support the paper's mechanistic story.
weaknesses: Absolute performance at the most aggressive settings (e.g., W4A3: IS 49.62 vs FP32 365.35, FID 33.47 vs 11.22) remains far from usable quality despite large relative improvements over a very weak baseline; the headline '467.73% IS improvement' framing can be seen as somewhat misleading given the still-poor absolute quality, and this should be more clearly contextualized rather than emphasized as a primary contribution metric.

The core technical novelty is incremental: it is essentially a design choice within Hadamard-based quantization (apply the transform only on the activation side, keep weights untouched) combined with an existing LoRA distillation framework and existing LSQ-style scale learning (from EfficientDM); the individual pieces (Hadamard for quantization, LoRA-QAT, timestep-aware scales) are all pre-existing, and the single-vs-double distinction, while sensible, is a relatively small conceptual delta over QuaRot/Xi et al.

Symmetric quantization is adopted for hardware-friendliness but the paper acknowledges this costs one effective bit versus asymmetric baselines like EfficientDM; a more careful controlled comparison isolating this trade-off (e.g., HQ-DM with asymmetric quantization) would clarify how much of the true gain comes from the Hadamard transform itself versus other confounds.

No wall-clock or hardware-measured demonstration of actual accelerated inference on real integer-arithmetic hardware/kernels; latency numbers in Table 6 appear to be simulated/estimated rather than from a genuine INT4 kernel implementation, which weakens the 'hardware-friendly' and speedup claims.

Missing comparisons with some claimed baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., DMQ, MPQ-DM, Xi et al.'s method directly) that specifically target outlier suppression in diffusion quantization, making it hard to assess whether HQ-DM outperforms the most relevant recent outlier-aware competitors rather than just EfficientDM and older PTQ methods.

The paper's clarity could be improved: notation is dense and somewhat inconsistent (e.g., tilde/hat notation for activations across the convolution formulation), and the manuscript lacks a discussion of limitations, failure modes, or societal impact.

Results at very aggressive bit-widths show still substantial variance and some metrics (e.g., sFID) are occasionally worse than baselines (e.g., Table 1 W4A4: HQ-DM sFID 9.60 vs EfficientDM's 9.80 is comparable, but in Table 2 W2/4 sFID is worse for HQ-DM), indicating the method's gains are not uniformly dominant across all metrics.

strengths: Clearly identifies a real, well-motivated limitation of prior Hadamard-based quantization work: the incompatibility of the conventional 'Double Hadamard Transformation' with integer convolution operations, and its tendency to amplify outliers in weight matrices. The proposed 'Single Hadamard Transformation' is a simple, mathematically well-explained fix supported by clear derivations (Eqs. 10-16) for both linear and convolutional layers.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple datasets (ImageNet 256x256, LSUN-Bedrooms, LSUN-Churches) and two distinct backbone families (UNet-based LDM and Transformer-based DiT), which strengthens generality claims.

Thorough component-wise ablation (Table 5) isolating the contributions of LSQ, LoRA distillation, and the Hadamard transformation, showing the transformation is beneficial even without the other components.
Direct head-to-head comparison between Single and Double Hadamard Transformation (Table 6) with both quality and latency metrics, directly substantiating the paper's central claim.
Strong gains are consistently observed in the most challenging low-bit regimes (e.g., W4A3, W4A4), which is the regime of greatest practical interest for deployment.
Reasonable coverage of related work situating the contribution against PTQ, QAT, and outlier-smoothing literature for diffusion models and LLMs.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat narrow: it largely amounts to restricting Hadamard transformation to activations only (avoiding an offline weight-side transform), combined with previously proposed LoRA-based distillation (EfficientDM) and LSQ. The conceptual leap beyond existing single-hadamard-for-activation ideas (e.g., in QuaRot-style approaches) is incremental.

The DHQ-DM baseline used for the Single vs Double comparison (Table 6) produces implausibly poor results even at W8A8 (IS ~5-6 vs. FP32's 365), which is a much larger degradation than one would expect from an outlier-amplification effect alone; this raises questions about whether the Double Hadamard baseline is a faithful/fair reimplementation of prior work or an under-tuned strawman, undermining confidence in the reported latency/quality advantage.

Absolute performance at the most aggressive setting (W4A3) remains far below full precision (IS 49.62 vs. 365.35; FID 33.47 vs. 11.22), so the large relative percentage improvements over EfficientDM are computed against an already very weak baseline and should be interpreted with caution.

Symmetric activation quantization is adopted for hardware-friendliness, but its cost (effectively one fewer usable bit versus asymmetric schemes used by baselines like EfficientDM) is acknowledged only qualitatively, without a controlled ablation isolating this effect from the Hadamard transformation's benefit.

Comparisons omit some recent outlier-aware diffusion PTQ methods explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., DMQ, MPQ-DM), which would have provided a more complete picture of the SOTA landscape at low-bit settings.

Latency/speedup measurement methodology (Table 6, Fig. 5c) is not described in sufficient detail (e.g., whether kernels are actual integer GEMM/conv implementations or simulated), limiting reproducibility of the hardware-efficiency claims.
No mention of code/model release, which affects reproducibility given the many implementation-specific details (block-diagonal Hadamard construction, per-timestep learnable scales, LoRA ranks, etc.).
